Verbos que pedem dativo: a pessoa vai pa: Verbs that take the dative: the person goes into the dative, step by step
PASSO 1: alguns verbos alemães pedem DAT: STEP 1: some German verbs put the person in the DATIVE, even though English uses a plain direct object: «Ich helfe dir» (I help you), «Ich danke dir» (I thank you), «Das Buch gehört mir» (the book belongs to me). STEP 2: these verbs do NOT take the accusative for the person: «Ich helfe dich» is wrong, even though "help you" feels like a direct object. STEP 3: learn each verb together with «wem?»: «helfen + dative», «danken + dative», «gehören + dative». A useful trick: think "give help TO you", "give thanks TO you", "belong TO me" — the "to" is your dative. STEP 4: «helfen» changes e to i with «du» and «er» (du hilfst, er hilft). STEP 5: «gratulieren» uses «zu» + dative for the occasion: «Ich gratuliere dir zum Geburtstag» (happy birthday — literally "I congratulate to you on the birthday"). STEP 6: «antworten» takes the dative for the person and «auf» + accusative for what you're answering: «Er antwortet dem Chef auf die E-Mail» (He answers the boss's e-mail).
em português dizemos «eu ajudo você» e «: English says "help him", "thank him", "answer him" with a direct object, so your instinct will say accusative (ihn). German keeps the old dative here: «Ich helfe ihm», «Ich danke ihm», «Ich antworte ihm». With «gehören», English already has the "to": "it belongs to me" = «es gehört mir».

Gefallen, schmecken, passen: o jeito ale: Gefallen, schmecken, passen: the German way of "liking"
PASSO 1: «gefallen» inverte a frase: que: STEP 1: «gefallen» flips the sentence: the person who likes goes into the DATIVE and the thing they like is the subject: «Das Kleid gefällt mir» — literally "the dress pleases me" = I like the dress. English does the same with "please" and "appeal to": "the dress appeals to me". STEP 2: the verb agrees with the THING: «Die Schuhe gefallen mir» (plural — "the shoes please me"). STEP 3: «schmecken» is about taste: «Die Suppe schmeckt mir (gut)» (I like the soup). STEP 4: «passen» means "to fit" and "to suit": «Die Jacke passt mir» (the jacket fits me), «Die Farbe passt dir gut» (the color suits you). STEP 5: «fehlen» (to be missing): «Mir fehlt Zeit» (I'm short of time — "time is missing to me"). STEP 6: «glauben», «folgen» and «zuhören» also take the dative for the person: «Ich glaube dir» (I believe you), «Sie folgt ihm» (she follows him), «Hör mir zu!» (listen to me!). STEP 7: «wehtun» (to hurt): «Der Kopf tut mir weh» (my head hurts). Careful: «gefallen» changes a to ä with «er» (es gefällt).
The person who likes goes into the dative.

«Mir ist kalt», «Wie geht es dir?»: sens: «Mir ist kalt», «Wie geht es dir?»: feelings with the dative
PASSO 1: para falar de SENSAÇÕES, o alem: STEP 1: to talk about how you FEEL, German puts the person in the dative and uses «sein» (or another verb) with an adjective: «Mir ist kalt» (I'm cold — literally "to me it is cold"), «Mir ist warm» (I'm warm), «Mir ist schlecht» (I feel sick), «Mir ist langweilig» (I'm bored). Saying «Ich bin kalt» means "I am a cold person"! STEP 2: to ask: «Ist dir kalt?» (Are you cold?) STEP 3: «Wie geht es dir?» (How are you?) and «Mir geht es gut» (I'm fine) use the same pattern. STEP 4: with the formal «Sie»: «Wie geht es Ihnen?» STEP 5: «Es tut mir leid» (I'm sorry): «Es tut mir leid, ich kann nicht kommen.»
